subject: science
intro: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Scientists learn about Earth's long history by studying rock strata, the layers of sedimentary rock. In undisturbed rock, deeper layers are older and layers near the top are younger. Fossils found in the layers help match rocks of the same age and show how life changed over time. The geologic time scale organizes this enormous history into named divisions (like eras and periods) so scientists can describe when events happened.

items.prompt: In undisturbed rock layers, which layer is oldest, the top or the bottom?

steps: Sedimentary layers form one on top of another over time.
The bottom layer formed first, so it is oldest.
So the bottom layer is oldest.

items.prompt: How can fossils in rock layers help scientists match rocks of the same age in different places?

steps: Certain fossils are found only in rocks of a certain age.
If the same fossil appears in two places, those rock layers formed at about the same time.
So fossils help match rocks of the same age.
solution.answer: Matching fossils indicate rock layers of the same age.

items.prompt: Why do scientists use a geologic time scale?

steps: Earth's history is about 4.6 billion years long, an enormous span.
The geologic time scale divides it into named parts like eras and periods.
This organizes the history so scientists can describe when events happened.
solution.answer: To organize Earth's enormous history into named divisions.

items.prompt: In undisturbed rock, where are the youngest layers?

steps: The youngest layers are near the top in undisturbed rock.
